passage: On Friday, Uma ma'am gathered the class in a circle for the safety drill. Each child stood and said a name, a home address and two phone numbers from a card. Ujjwal's knees felt wobbly, but he read in a steady voice: his flat number, the lane, Papa's number and Kaur aunty's number from next door. "And what do you do if your grandmother falls and nobody else is home?" Uma ma'am asked. "Call 112," said Ujjwal. "I say my address and stay on the line. Then I call Kaur aunty." The girl beside him forgot her lane, and Uma ma'am gave her time to try again. Ujjwal put the card back in his bag pocket.

qa.a: Ujjwal read Kaur aunty's number from next door.

qa.a: She could practise her address and numbers until she can say them without stopping, using the card for support.

qa.a: Uma ma'am gives her time to try again, so she does not feel judged while she is learning.

passage: I live in the flat opposite Gurleen's, so I was in the corridor when Ajji from 4B slipped by the lift, near the wet mop. She sat on the floor, holding her hip, gasping. My mind went blank. Gurleen, who is ten, dropped her school bag, said, "Ajji, we are here," and dialled 112. She gave the building name, floor and flat number without stopping, and said, "She fell. She is awake." Then she told me, "Go and knock on Mehta uncle's door." She looked calm, though I could not tell if she was scared. Later I saw a card in her bag pocket with the numbers written out. Naveen

Rashmi: "Sonali, emergency practice. What's our home address?"
Sonali: "Flat 4B, Gulmohar Apartments, Station Road, Nagpur."
Rashmi: "And the emergency number?"
Sonali: "112."
Rashmi: "If Mumma falls and doesn't wake up, what do you do first?"
Sonali: "Call 112. Say our address. Say what happened."
Rashmi: "Then?"
Sonali: "Call Nani. Her number's on the fridge. Then open the door for the ambulance."
Rashmi: "And if you get scared?"
Sonali: "I say the steps out loud. One, two, three."
Rashmi: "Good. We practise every Sunday because when you're scared, your brain goes blank. The steps don't."

subtype: Learning emergency numbers and who to tell [Actor]
passage: I'm Kashish, and when I was nine, my Nani, Indu, slipped in the bathroom while Mummy was at work. She was on the floor and couldn't get up, and she was holding her hip. My hands were shaking. For a second I couldn't think at all. Then I heard Mummy's voice in my head, from all our practice. "112. Address. What happened." I dialled. I said, "My Nani fell. She can't get up. House number 17, Lane 3, Sector 9." The lady on the phone told me to stay with Nani and not move her. Then I called Mummy, whose number I knew by heart. The ambulance came. Nani says I was braver than her.

qa.q: Where did Nani slip?
qa.a: In the bathroom.

qa.q: How did Kashish feel when Nani fell?
qa.a: Kashish felt frightened, hands shaking, unable to think for a second.

qa.q: What helped Kashish act despite the fear?
qa.a: The practised steps, 112, address, what happened, came back, and knowing Mummy's number by heart.

qa.q: How might Nani have felt as Kashish made the call?
qa.a: Nani, in pain and unable to get up, likely felt relieved and grateful that Kashish knew exactly what to do.

subtype: Learning emergency numbers and who to tell [Actor]
passage:
Class teacher's note, Class 4, after the safety drill.
Today we practised what to do in an emergency at home. Each child had to say the emergency number, their full address and the name and number of a trusted adult. Akash knew all three instantly; he told us his family practises at dinner. Chinmay knew the number but stumbled on his address and did not know any adult's phone number by heart. He looked embarrassed. I reassured him that this is exactly why we practise. I have sent a note home asking families to help each child learn their address and one adult's number. We will repeat the drill in two weeks.

qa.q: What three things did each child have to say?
qa.a: The emergency number, their full address and the name and number of a trusted adult.

qa.q: How did Chinmay feel when he stumbled on his address?
qa.a: He looked embarrassed at not knowing it by heart.

qa.q: What is the teacher doing to help, and why does it matter?
qa.a: Sending a note home and repeating the drill, because rehearsed steps work when fear stops a child from thinking.

qa.q: How might Akash's family routine help him in a real emergency?
qa.a: Practising at dinner means Akash can recall the steps instantly even if he is frightened.

grounding: A teacher's note shows children rehearsing emergency numbers, addresses and a trusted adult to call.

passage:
Sunday
Today I was so scared my hands shook. Dadi slipped in the bathroom and couldn't get up. She said, "Eshaan, don't pull me, call someone." My head went empty. Then I remembered the card on the fridge that Mama makes us practise every Sunday: 1. Tell a grown-up close by. 2. Call Papa. 3. If it's serious, 112. I ran next door and banged on Baljeet uncle's door. He came with his phone, called 112 and told them our address, Flat 3, Gulmohar Colony. I called Papa like we practised. The ambulance people were kind. Dadi is okay now, just a sore wrist. Baljeet uncle said I did everything right. I think the practising did it, not me being brave.

qa.q: What was the third step on the card on the fridge?
qa.a: If it's serious, 112.

qa.q: How did Eshaan feel when Dadi slipped?
qa.a: Eshaan was so scared that the hands shook and the mind went empty.

qa.q: What helped Eshaan act even though fear made thinking hard?
qa.a: The card practised every Sunday: the steps came back in order, so Eshaan fetched Baljeet uncle and called Papa.

qa.q: How might Dadi feel about what Eshaan did?
qa.a: Dadi was probably relieved and proud that Eshaan didn't pull her and quickly got a grown-up.
